clinicalPearls: Superwarfarins such as brodifacoum are far more potent and vastly longer acting than warfarin, so coagulopathy can persist for weeks to months
Coagulopathy is delayed, typically appearing a day or two after ingestion, because existing clotting factors must first be depleted
A single acute exploratory ingestion by a child rarely causes clinically significant coagulopathy, whereas large or repeated ingestion can
Consider covert or intentional exposure in an adult with unexplained prolonged coagulation and no prescribed anticoagulant
Bleeding can be occult, so haematuria, bruising, gum bleeding, gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage should prompt assessment of coagulation
Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) is the specific antidote and must often be continued in high oral doses for a prolonged period given the long half-life
Acute major bleeding is treated with factor replacement such as prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma in addition to vitamin K
Prophylactic vitamin K should not be started routinely after a trivial ingestion, as it can mask evolving coagulopathy; the INR is followed instead
reference.pathophysiology: Superwarfarins inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, the enzyme that regenerates reduced vitamin K, which is the essential cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and of proteins C and S. Without functional vitamin K these factors cannot be activated, producing an anticoagulant state. Because factor VII has the shortest half-life, the prothrombin time and INR prolong first, but full coagulopathy is delayed until preformed factors are consumed. Unlike warfarin, superwarfarins are highly lipophilic, extensively tissue-bound and slowly eliminated, so their anticoagulant effect is markedly prolonged.
additionalDifferentials: Direct oral anticoagulant or heparin effect
Liver disease with impaired synthetic function
Vitamin K deficiency from malabsorption or poor intake
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and INR, measured serially over an appropriate delayed window
Activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen
Full blood count to assess for anaemia from blood loss
Specific clotting factor assays and mixing studies where the cause is unclear
Superwarfarin concentration in plasma where available to confirm and monitor
Investigations for the site of bleeding, including imaging when haemorrhage is suspected
redFlags: Active bleeding, especially intracranial or gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Markedly prolonged INR with clinical bleeding
Large deliberate ingestion or repeated exposure
Rebound coagulopathy when vitamin K is reduced or stopped too early
reference.prognosis: With adequate and sustained vitamin K therapy and treatment of any acute bleeding, prognosis is generally good, although therapy and monitoring may be required for weeks to months; life-threatening haemorrhage before treatment carries significant risk.
pitfalls: Checking coagulation only at presentation and missing delayed coagulopathy
Stopping vitamin K prematurely and allowing rebound anticoagulation
Giving prophylactic vitamin K after a trivial ingestion, masking evolving coagulopathy
Relying on vitamin K alone in major bleeding rather than replacing clotting factors
Failing to consider covert or intentional poisoning in unexplained coagulopathy
management: Give vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) as the specific antidote, typically in high oral doses continued for a prolonged period because of the drug's long half-life
Reverse active or life-threatening haemorrhage urgently with prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma
Consider activated charcoal for a recent substantial ingestion presenting early
Monitor prothrombin time and INR serially over an extended window, titrating and tapering vitamin K to the coagulation response rather than treating pre-emptively
Identify and manage the site of bleeding and provide transfusion support where anaemia results
Arrange psychiatric assessment for intentional ingestion and a safeguarding review for childhood exposure, and identify the source
Involve clinical toxicology and haematology in ongoing management
